topic.title: 6 ways billionaires avoid paying tax, explained

title: 6 ways billionaires avoid paying tax, explained
description:
How can someone worth billions pay less tax than a teacher, and do it legally?
Sharma Uncle walks Rohan through six moves the very rich use: shares instead of salary (and the one-dollar paycheque), borrowing instead of selling, the reset at death, the family foundation, losses against gains, and the one move almost anyone can copy.
Every figure is computed, every assumption said out loud, and the catches are in there too.

Chapters
0:00 Intro
0:20 Shares, not salary
1:55 Borrow, don't sell
3:28 The reset
4:47 The foundation
5:43 Losers vs winners
6:46 The one you can copy

An animated story with illustrative numbers; the characters are not advisers.
Speak to a licensed financial adviser in your country before making financial decisions.

lines.text: Rohan earns $75,000, and the tax man takes $7,670. Sharma's shares grew $100.0M this year. His tax on that? Nothing. And it's all legal.
Hold on. How does a man worth billions pay less tax than me?
Six legal moves. Shares, not salary. Borrow, don't sell. The reset. The foundation. Losers against winners. And the last one, which you can copy.
Move one. Shares, not salary.
Rohan's money arrives as a payslip. Before he even sees it, the tax comes out.
On $75,000 a year, his federal income tax is $7,670. He keeps $67,330.
Every single month. I never even get to touch that part.
A teacher, a nurse, a driver. Everyone paid by payslip lives by the same rule: earn it, and it's taxed.
Even my overtime gets taxed before I see a cent of it.
Sharma barely takes a salary. His wealth sits in shares of the company he built.
This year those shares grew by 10%. On paper, he is $100.0M richer.
I won't earn that much in my whole life.
And the tax on that gain this year? Nothing. In America, a gain on shares is taxed when you sell, not while it grows.
So if he never sells, he never pays?
Not on the growth. Your tax comes out before you see your pay. Mine waits until I choose to sell.
Why would I pay myself a big salary, beta? Salary is one of the most heavily taxed kinds of money there is.
When Steve Jobs returned to Apple, he famously took a salary of just a single dollar a year.
Income tax on a single dollar a year? Nothing at all. That salary is pure symbolism.
So he worked for free? That's actually kind of noble.
Noble, and clever. His fortune was already in shares. A big salary is taxed every month, at up to 37%.
One honest detail. Shares paid as wages, like stock awards, are usually taxed as income. The shares a founder started with were never wages.
That's the gap between earning money and owning things that grow.
So Rohan is taxed on every payslip, before a single dollar reaches him.
And Sharma is taxed on his gains only when he sells, and only when he decides.
That's the whole game. A salary gets taxed every month. Shares can grow for decades with no tax on the gain, only on any dividends.
But Sharma still needs cash to live on. Selling would wake the tax man. So he does something stranger.
Move two. Borrow, don't sell.
Sharma wants $100,000,000 to spend. The obvious way is to sell some shares.
If he sells $100,000,000 of shares that are pure gain, the tax man takes $23.8M.
That's 23.8%: the top federal rate on long-term gains, plus the investment surtax.
Sell, and hand over that much? Never. I'll take a loan instead.
The bank hands him a loan of $100,000,000, with his shares pledged as the guarantee.
The bank lends him that much? They won't even raise my card limit.
Banks like this kind of loan. It's backed by shares they can sell if he ever stops paying.
And here's the trick. A loan is not income. So there is no income tax on it.
That borrowed cash pays for the houses, the travel and the parties. None of it counts as income, because it never was.
But a loan isn't free. He pays interest on every dollar of it.
True. At an assumed 5% a year, the interest is $5.0M a year.
Put them side by side. Tax if he sells: $23.8M. Interest for a year: $5.0M. The tax bill is 4.8× bigger, though the interest comes back every year.
So borrowing beats selling, as long as the shares grow faster than the interest.
Meanwhile the shares he kept keep growing. At an assumed 8% a year, in 10 years they could be worth $215.9M.
The loan costs me interest. The shares earn me more. And the tax man just waits.
The trick was never the loan, beta. The trick is never needing to sell.
So the richer you are, the cheaper it gets to borrow. Got it.
The catch: if the shares crash, the bank can demand more security, or sell them for him at the worst moment.
Year one, he borrows. Year five, he borrows again. Year ten, his pile is bigger than ever, and he has never sold a share.
Two moves down. But who pays back the loan? That's the strangest move of all.
Move three. The reset.
He buys young. He holds through every crash. He borrows in old age. And then he passes it all on.
Sharma bought his first shares for almost nothing. Today they are worth $1,000,000,000.
Almost every dollar of that is gain. If he sold it all at 23.8%, the tax would be $238.0M.
So I don't sell. I hold, I borrow, and I keep holding for the rest of my life.
Here's why that matters. A gain is measured from your starting price, called the basis. Normally that's what you paid.
When he passes away, his will leaves the shares to his children.
And their starting price resets to what the shares are worth on that day.
So the gain from his whole lifetime? It is never taxed as a gain. It's wiped clean.
That can't be legal.
It is. It's called the step-up in basis, and it's been in the tax code for a century.
His children could sell the next day and owe almost no capital gains tax.
And all those loans? His estate can pay them off by selling some shares, at the new price, with little gain left to tax.
So the loans get repaid, and the gain still never gets taxed. Buy, borrow, die.
Buy, borrow, die. Tax advisers really do call it that.
There is a catch. Above $15,000,000 per person, the estate can owe estate tax, at up to 40%.
For most families, estate tax never comes up at all. Their estates are far smaller than that.
And the reset isn't only for the rich. It applies to anyone who inherits, even a small house or a few shares.
Which is why people like me plan for it early. With trusts, and with gifts to charity.
And the most famous of those gifts has the family's own name on the door.
Move four. The foundation.
Three moves done. The fourth starts with a gift.
Sharma gives $500,000,000 of shares to his own family foundation.
He just gave all of that away?
Why shares and not cash? Cash has already been taxed. Shares full of gain have not.
A gift is not a sale. So the $119.0M of tax on their gain is never paid.
And I can deduct the gift from my income, within the limits. Generous, and useful.
My accountant calls it doing well by doing good.
Bill Gates and Warren Buffett have both given away billions of dollars in shares to foundations.
But the foundation is his family's. His family can run it, and choose where the money goes.
So he gives it away, and somehow still keeps it?
Not quite. By law, it must hand out about 5% of its assets every year in grants. Here, that's $25.0M.
The grants go out. The rest stays invested and can keep growing. And his children can run it after him.
The money does reach good causes. Slowly, on the family's terms, and with their name on it.
So the rich even get a tax break for being generous. Of course they do.
Four moves down. The next one, he can use every December.
Move five. Losers against winners.
This year Sharma sold a winner, a stock with $10,000,000 of gain. Tax due: $2.4M.
But he also owns a loser. A stock that fell by the same amount.
So he sells the loser too, and on paper the loss cancels the gain.
Gain: $10,000,000. Loss: the same. Taxable gain left this year: nothing. His tax bill this year drops by $2.4M.
And a loss bigger than his gains doesn't vanish. It can carry forward, to cancel gains in later years.
Selling something at a loss, on purpose? That sounds completely backwards.
The loss was already there. Selling just makes it count. Then I buy something similar, never the same stock within a month.
Buy back the same stock too soon, and the rules disallow the loss. It's called the wash-sale rule.
Every December, I look for what's down. Then I put those losses to work.
And this one isn't only for billionaires. Anyone with a taxable investing account can use losses the same way.
Losses are part of investing. This just makes them sting a little less.
So losing money can cut his tax bill. My brain hurts.
That's five moves. But look closely at what every single one of them needs.
Every move needs the same thing: a fortune already sitting in shares. Rohan has a payslip. But the last move works with a payslip too.
Move six. The one you can copy.
Billionaires let their money grow untaxed for decades. Ordinary people get a version of that too.
In America it's called a Roth account. You put in money from your pay that's already been taxed.
Then it grows. And when you take it out in retirement, if you follow the rules, the growth is tax-free.
The trade is simple. You pay tax on the money going in, so you never pay it on the growth coming out.
Hold on. Someone like me can actually do that?
So I pay the tax now, while my income is small, and never on decades of growth?
Most people with earned income can, under limits. Other countries have their own versions, like the ISA in Britain.
Many employers also offer a retirement plan at work, and some add money of their own to what you put in.
I opened mine at your age, with very little. Time did most of the work.
But a small amount every month can't turn into anything big, can it?
It can. And the earlier he starts, the more years the growth gets to work.
Say Rohan puts $500 a month into his nest egg, for 30 years.
He sets it to move on payday, automatically, so the money is saved before he can spend it.
After 10 years, the pot is $92,083. Most of that is still money he put in himself.
It's move one again, at Rohan's size: money that grows untaxed, for a very long time.
Year one, it's small. Year ten, it starts to grow on its own. By year thirty, the growth is doing most of the work.
Over the years he puts in $180,000. At an assumed 8% a year, it grows to $750,148. And the tax on all that growth, when he takes it out? None.
The catch: there are income limits, a yearly cap on what goes in, and the money is meant to stay put until retirement.
That's $570,148 of growth he never pays tax on. The same idea as the billionaires, at Rohan's size.
Six moves. Five of them need a fortune. The last one only needs time.
So the rich don't pay less by breaking the rules. They know which money gets taxed, and when.
Simplified maths: United States federal tax only, with assumed rates. Which move surprised you most? Comment below.

Title (plan.json title and topic.title, script title, thumbnail if it repeats it): 'Every way billionaires avoid paying tax, explained' promises more than the video shows. It covers seven moves and leaves out well-known ones (GRATs/dynasty trusts beyond a passing mention, QSBS, real-estate depreciation, carried interest). Retitle to the count the video delivers, e.g. '7 ways billionaires avoid paying tax, explained' (or 'How billionaires legally avoid tax: 7 moves').

Beat c5-saved: 'He just saved $2.4M' overstates tax-loss harvesting. Selling the loser and buying something similar resets his starting price lower, so the tax is generally deferred, not erased (unless he holds to death, move three). Say it cuts this year's bill instead, e.g. 'Taxable gain left this year: nothing. His tax bill this year drops by $2.4M.' Adjust the matching stats card label if it says 'saved'.
